items_missed: No agenda statement and no 'sound good?' confirmation. The call opened 'Hello, good morning this is Halene with ein moving. How can I help you?' and went straight to 'Okay ma'am, what is your name please?' then 'what are the clarifications that you'd like to ask?' — the customer set the agenda, not the rep. No timeframe, no roadmap, no explicit confirmation.
Never asked 'how are you today?' or any warm-up question.

Save Your Ass speech: completely absent, and the customer handed her the opening verbatim. She asked 'is there anything else that I need to do in preparation for like the move' and Jeline answered 'Not thing ma'am, because you'll handle the boxes, right?... I don't think you really have to do anything prior the move day.' That is the exact inverse of the prep speech on a job where prep is the only lever left. No 'prep = shorter move = lower bill,' no consolidation examples (drawers, photos on walls, loose items), no 'take a carload' tip, no 'does that make sense?' close.

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned. The inventory is an adjustable bed frame she admits she'll have to partially dismantle, a sectional, and a mirror, down an elevator and across town — and the $2,000 coverage never came up once, not even when the customer asked what's included.

On-Time Guarantee never mentioned, despite Jeline being the one to set the window: 'Our schedule ma'am is between 8:30 AM to 9:00 AM. Are you okay with that arrival window?' That is the natural place for it and it was skipped.
No 'pricing is super simple' opener — she led with 'let's talk about now the estimate here ma'am.'

'No hidden fees' pitch only half-delivered. She said 'everything is included here and no heat [hidden] and fees of any type' but never enumerated the differentiators — no credit card fees, no transportation fees, no fuel surcharge, no assembly fees — even though the customer explicitly teed it up: 'I've seen some other companies that they gave you an estimate but then they charge you like gas and all these things miles.'

No deposit never stated as a differentiator. The customer asked 'How does payment work? Like, do I pay like before or it goes after?' — the perfect opening — and Jeline explained pay-on-completion and card-only, but never said the words 'there's no deposit required to hold the date.'

Clock start never explained — no 'the clock starts on-site when we open the contract.' The 2.5-hour minimum and the 15-minute increments were both covered, but the customer never learned when billing begins.

No sense-check, and it cost her: the customer restated the billing as 'so you charge $1,550 for every fifteen minutes, that goes after' and Jeline replied 'Yes, ma'am. That is correct.' Whatever the transcription garble, the customer's read of the increment was confirmed without being restated back cleanly. A booked job now rests on an unverified understanding of the overage rate.

Drive time never explained as billable. Origin 1370 Lyn St to 12489 Research Blvd is a real cross-town leg and was never named as part of the hours — she attributed the whole 2.5–3.0 range to walk-distance uncertainty alone.

Elevator/stairs never explained as a time variable. The customer raised it herself — 'that can take time as well for like loading unloading depending on the access' — and got 'Okay. Alright sir.' in reply.

Estimate anchored to the floor of the range while she was openly admitting she had no walk-distance data: 'since, again we're not yet sure with the distance... I'm really thinking that this could be only within our minimum hours of two and a half.' Two second-floor apartments, elevator waits both ends, an unknown carry the customer guessed at 'two or three' school buses, a sectional, an adjustable base needing partial teardown, plus the drive — $500–600 is optimistic, and this is the estimate-accuracy rock's exact failure mode (underestimating apartments).
Saturday rate tier never addressed. She quoted a flat '$200 per hour for two movers' and then booked 'Saturday September 19th' without confirming whether weekend pricing differs.

Never asked about additional stops, storage stops, or additional rooms (garage, balcony, storage unit). The customer volunteered her inventory unprompted, which papered over the gap, but the questions were never asked.
No moving-stressor question. She never asked 'is there anything you're particularly worried about with this move?' — the customer's one clear anxiety (the adjustable bed) she had to raise herself.
Insurance never actually explained — mentioned only as a word inside the included list ('gas and truck taxes, insurance'). No No Worries, no 60¢/lb baseline.
'Any other questions before I let you go?' never asked, and hours / how to reach us never given. Every question in the back half of the call came from the customer.
Customer's name never used once. She spelled it out — 'N-A-D-I-A-Q-U-I-N-T-A-N-I double LA' — and Jeline said 'Okay, thank you' and then used 'ma'am' roughly thirty times instead of 'Nadia.'
Misgendered the customer twice mid-call — 'Alright sir.' and 'Yes sir mm-hmm that is correct.' — on a call where she had the profile open.
top_strength: This is the best walk-distance probe in the batch. Rather than accepting 'I wouldn't know how to calculate it,' Jeline reached for the equivalent: 'let's imagine length of a call be ma'am. Like, how many school bus do you think would it take if we're going to use the front entrance?' and when that still stalled she pushed once more for the operational answer — 'But then ma'am personally you'd recommend if we use the back entrance' — got the customer to walk her through the loading-dock-to-elevator-to-sidewalk route, and closed it with 'Okay, understood. I'll just Notate that here.' She then ran the same probe on the destination. That is textbook Section 5 variable work and it is why her range was a range and not a single number. She also closed the call the way the scorecard wants: she asked for the business live ('Alright, so, I'll confirm this booking now for you'), collected both unit numbers before booking, delivered a complete and specific email handoff — 'on that email there will be a bolted list. It will be the date and time that we agreed upon the addresses and the contact information. So if everything is correct just reply to that email' — and landed Meet Your Mover cleanly and proactively: 'a few days before your move ma'am you will receive an email introducing the movers to you so you know her faces.' Customer's own verdict: 'thank you so much. You've been so helpful.'
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix, and it is a single sentence: the customer literally asked 'is there anything else that I need to do in preparation for like the move' and Jeline said no. That is the Save Your Ass section being declined on request — a full 10 points, and on a time-billed job it is the one thing that protects both the customer's bill and Einstein's estimate accuracy. The line she needed was: 'Great question, Nadia — this is actually where you can save yourself real money. Everything you can consolidate before we get there makes the move shorter and the bill lower. Get the loose stuff out of your nightstand and dresser drawers, take the mirror and anything small in a carload yourself if you can, and have the bed stripped and the sectional cushions off so we can wrap and go the second we walk in. Does that make sense?' Practice that as a reflex answer to 'do I need to do anything?' — the correct answer is never 'nothing.' Second priority: she booked a job with an adjustable bed frame she has to partially dismantle, a sectional, and a mirror, and never said the words No Worries. When the customer asked 'you said that everything's already included, correct?' the answer should have been 'Correct — and that includes our No Worries Damage Coverage, up to $2,000 per move to repair, replace, or reimburse anything we accidentally damage. That covers the adjustable base and the mirror.' Same gap on the On-Time Guarantee: she set an 8:30–9:00 window herself and let it pass without 'and if we miss that window we start discounting immediately.' Two things to fix in EMMA today, both of them booking risks rather than coaching notes: (1) the overage rate is confirmed wrong or at best unverified on the recording — the customer said 'so you charge $1,550 for every fifteen minutes' and got 'Yes, ma'am. That is correct.' Listen to that exchange and send a written correction before move day; this is a billing dispute waiting to happen on Sept 19. (2) The estimate is anchored to the 2.5-hour minimum while Jeline was on record saying she didn't know the walk distance, on a second-floor-to-second-floor elevator move with a cross-town drive and an adjustable base. Drive time was never counted at all. Re-run this quote with drive time and elevator staging in it before the confirmation goes out — this is precisely the apartment-underestimate pattern the estimate-accuracy rock is chasing, and it is a bottom-4-style case study sitting in a single call. Smaller but visible: use the customer's name — she spelled it letter by letter and never heard it back — and check the profile for gender before 'Alright sir.'
phone_presence_notes: Patient and reassuring in the right moments ('Okay, ma'am no worries,' and she stayed with the walk-distance question without making the customer feel dumb about not knowing) and the customer closed with 'you've been so helpful' — but the warmth was generic rather than personal: dozens of 'ma'am' and long runs of 'Mm-hmm' filler, the customer's name never used once after she spelled it, and two 'sir' slips on a female customer.
audio_review_reason: The pricing exchange needs to be heard, not read. The transcript has the customer saying '$1,550 for every fifteen minutes' and Jeline confirming 'Yes, ma'am. That is correct,' plus '$600 $50' and 'no heat and fees of any type' — all three are likely transcription artifacts, but one of them is the overage rate on a job that is now booked, so the actual spoken numbers have to be verified before the confirmation email is treated as accurate. Also worth confirming how the rep's own name landed on the greeting ('this is Halene').
